public_rationale: The sources point toward the contextual reading: NIST's safety framework was voluntary, and the later CRS survey describes limited federal AI legislation. But these records do not establish the complete legal position on the post date. California court materials also show why 'any chatbot they want' should not be treated as literal freedom from all legal duties. The evidence retrieved is insufficient for a supported or contradicted outcome under the stated safety-approval criterion.
limitations: Several relevant official pages could not be read and were excluded as evidence.
The cited legal materials are guidance and summaries, not a complete historical survey of operative requirements.
A literal absence-of-any-law reading would produce a different assessment from the contextual safety-approval reading.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Right now AI is basically the Wild West, in that anyone can post any chatbot they want.

statement.excerpt: Right now, as I have said before, the AI is basically the Wild West; anyone can post any chatbot they want.

from_speaker: anyone can post any chatbot they want
Congress needs to to find out what happened, and start placing some restrictions
our_interpretation: The reference to Congress makes the United States the relevant jurisdiction.

The pharmaceutical comparison and discussion of public releases make the ordinary reading an absence of a general mandatory safety-review or approval requirement before releasing a general-purpose chatbot.
I do not read 'basically' as claiming immunity from every existing law governing fraud, privacy, disclosures, or specialized activities.
The target is the legal position on the publication date, 2023-02-20. A legal state can be checked as of that day without substituting a financial reporting period.
criteria.support_condition: A historical legal review establishes that, on 2023-02-20, developers could generally release general-purpose chatbots to the U.S. public without mandatory government safety review or approval.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Binding requirements in force on 2023-02-20 required general-purpose chatbot developers to obtain safety review or approval before public release. Rules limited to particular conduct or specialized uses would qualify the broad wording but would not alone refute this reading.

evidence.locator: Page 20, paragraph introducing the AI RMF Playbook
evidence.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
evidence.explanation: NIST's own guidance identifies both the framework and its playbook as voluntary. This supports the direction of Marcus's observation but cannot establish the absence of requirements under other laws.

evidence.locator: Federal Laws Addressing AI, concluding sentence before State AI Laws
evidence.publisher: Congressional Research Service, reproduced by EveryCRSReport.com
evidence.explanation: The CRS survey describes the limited reach of federal AI legislation. Its later assessment does not by itself establish every federal and state release requirement on 2023-02-20, so it is context only.

evidence.locator: Appendix E: Example of Chatbot Disclosure, Privacy Policy, and Disclaimer
evidence.explanation: These official materials show that bot-related legal duties were recognized before the post. They qualify a literal claim of complete legal freedom, but describe disclosure rather than government safety approval.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A sourced historical legal survey establishing whether general-purpose chatbot releases required mandatory safety review or approval under federal or applicable state law on 2023-02-20, with specialized-use restrictions identified separately.
